messages.author: f874fa23d6c8063d
messages.subject: procD.lm and pairwise
parts:
Hello Geomorph users,

I am trying to use procD.lm to compare the shapes between the groups in my data set while accounting for sex. In my data I have members from three different artificial selection lines spanning three generations during the selection process (beginning, middle an end). What I am trying to do is pretty simple (I think) I just want to compare the mean shapes of all nine groups. I expect that random bred controls will not differ in shape over the selection process and I expect that none of the founder populations will differ because selection has not been applied. So I concatenate line and generation into a nine level variable using (Line:Generation) called Groups. If I run the code below I get that all 9 groups differ significantly, which is a bit odd if you saw the PCA.

Groups <- Line:Gen

shape_lm <- procD.lm(shape~group, iter = 999, RRPP = T,  SS.type = c("III"),  effect.type = c("F"))
summary(shape_lm)
pw <- pairwise(shape_lm, groups = Groups)
summary(pw, confidence =0.95, test.type = "dist)

If I add sex as a co-variate I will get one or more groups differs significantly and sex accounts for a small but significant amount of variation. However, if I now take this new model with the co-variate and put it into pairwise() I get a response that says no groups differ despite what the summary of the procD.lm says. The code is written out below.

shape_lm_2 <- procD.lm(shape~group + sex, iter = 999, RRPP = T,  SS.type = c("III"),  effect.type = c("F")) )
summary(shape_lm_2)
pw_2 <- pairwise(shape_lm_2, groups = Groups)
summary(pw_2, confidence =0.95, test.type = "dist)

I am pretty new to morphometrics and multivariate stats I am finding the vignette/ help are a bit inaccessible. I think the problem might be something to do with the null that pairwise is using? Reveal.model.designs(shape_lm_2) tells me this, but I am not sure how to interpret it:

           Reduced         Full                                  
group      sex         group + sex                                  
sex        group       group + sex  <-  Null/Full inherent in pairwise

Any insights would be greatly appreciated! If anyone has advice or could suggest some reading I could do that would be awesome!

Cheers,
Cole

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] procD.lm and pairwise
parts:
Cole,

If you have questions about the results, it might help to include them.  Indicating “significant” or “non-significant” doesn’t help anybody to understand if the effects are large or small.  It is possible to get a small but significant overall effect that does not translate to any significant pairwise differences.  Just a guess without looking at any results, like an ANOVA table.

Mike

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] procD.lm and pairwise
parts:
Cole,

The issue is that you did not define a null model in your pairwise test, so the function must use what it thinks could be the null model based on your procD.lm fit.  In this case, it used an illogical model.  The reveal.model.designs function tells you which null model/full model comparison pairwise will use if you leave it up to the function to guess.  Even though you used type III SS, it uses the order of variables to guess.  In your case the null model has group as a factor and the full model, group + sex as factors.  Therefore, you are testing for group differences after holding group variation constant.  There is no way to find a significant test result that way.

You can do one of two things.

1) Create another procD.lm fit with shape ~ sex, and define this as the null model in pairwise
2) Change the order in shape_lm_2 to be shape ~ sex + group

The second option merely tricks pairwise; the first option means you take control of defining what the null model should be.

The reason that a null model does not have to be defined in pairwise is that it is computationally quite a bit faster if you can rely on the random outcomes already generated from procD.lm.  Generally speaking, that might work well with type I SS and some a priori reasoning given to term order; it is less-straightforward with type III SS.  It is always best to define the null model so you know exactly on which expectation — like sexual dimorphism — you are conditioning your results.

Hope that helps!
Mike
